title: Marginal Benefit of Deterministic Generate–Verify–Repair Guards for LLM‑Generated NetOps Configurations: A Paired Emulator Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory experiment (study_id cnd-001-5f3a) to measure whether a bounded, deterministic generate–verify–repair (GVR) guard improves emulator-executable success for LLM-generated network configurations under a shared-candidate generation budget. For each of n = 200 natural‑language NetOps intents a single initial candidate from gpt-5-mini was used for both arms: the baseline ungated acceptance and the guarded deterministic three‑stage validator plus a rule‑based deterministic repair applied only when unambiguous and within a preregistered repair_budget ≤ 1. Primary, artifact-backed outcomes: baseline = 199/200 (0.995), guarded = 200/200 (1.000); paired contingency n11 = 199, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. The preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar (two‑sided binomial on discordant pairs) yields p = 1.0. Complementary paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.015]. The preregistered 0.15 absolute‑effect target is excluded by the observed CI because the baseline success rate was near ceiling. We also provide two artifact‑grounded clarifications requested during review: the aggregated difficulty counts across the confirmatory bank (easy=20, medium=80, hard=60, very_hard=40) and an auditable exemplar of the single repaired episode (task_id task-000137; validator code MISSING_REQUIRED_COMMAND; deterministic transformation: insertion of the missing required command at the canonical position; validation_before.valid == false → validation_after.valid == true). All analysis and execution accounting reported here are artifact‑backed in the archived study bundle.

sections.introduction: Automating routine network operations (NetOps) changes with large language models (LLMs) promises reduced manual effort but raises an operational‑safety question: do LLM‑produced configurations execute correctly when applied to control planes? Prior intent‑to‑configuration work demonstrates that LLMs can synthesize vendor‑like CLI commands from natural‑language intents but also documents systematic structural and semantic errors (e.g., missing required commands, unsafe ordering, or protected‑field modification). Proposed mitigations include retrieval‑augmentation, constrained decoding, verifier‑assisted repair, and multi‑stage tool augmentation; yet empirical, execution‑grounded evidence quantifying the marginal benefit of applying a bounded deterministic repair to the same initial LLM candidate under strict hosted‑call budgets remains limited. We preregistered and ran a paired experiment (study_id cnd-001-5f3a) that isolates the “repair‑on‑same‑candidate” question by sharing a single initial LLM candidate across both arms (baseline = accept candidate; guarded = validate then deterministically repair if unambiguous). This shared‑candidate estimand addresses practical deployment constraints—hosted calls can be costly or governed—and therefore answers whether a conservative, auditable validator plus a single deterministic repair meaningfully increases the proportion of emulator‑executable configurations without additional LLM calls. Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation under the shared‑candidate estimand; (2) concise algorithmic descriptions and operational constraints of the deterministic three‑stage validator and the deterministic, rule‑based repair operator used in the guarded pipeline; (3) complete execution accounting and exact‑test justification suitable for small discordant counts; and (4) two artifact‑grounded clarifications requested during review (aggregate difficulty distribution and an auditable repaired exemplar).
sections.related_work: Prior literature splits into three strands relevant to this study. First, intent‑to‑configuration research demonstrates feasibility and documents error modes: LLMs synthesize device‑style CLI sequences from natural intents but often produce structural inconsistencies or omit required commands; prototype evaluations report promising but imperfect results in curated settings (Nguyen et al., 2024). Second, mitigation strategies developed in NetOps and adjacent structured‑generation domains include retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG), live schema grounding (SAL), constrained/grammar‑aware decoding, and verifier‑assisted repair; these reduce hallucination and format errors in tasks such as NL2SQL and document‑grounded generation but require careful domain adaptation to vendor CLI dialects and operational policies (Mishra et al.; constrained‑decoding literature). Third, deterministic verifiers and emulator‑backed validators provide an assurance layer: formal‑methods tools (NetKAT variants, weighted NetKAT) and emulator checks detect many semantic violations prior to deployment, though they do not fully capture dynamic runtime effects (e.g., BGP convergence timing) or device firmware idiosyncrasies. Our study sits at the intersection of these strands by empirically measuring, under a constrained‑call practical estimand, the marginal yield of a conservative GVR guard applied to the same initial LLM candidate.
sections.methodology:
Design and preregistration: The study was preregistered (study_id cnd-001-5f3a) as a paired design with shared_initial_candidate generation. For each of 200 curated natural‑language intents the hosted model (requested: gpt‑5‑mini) produced a single initial candidate. That candidate constituted both the baseline arm (ungated acceptance) and the guarded arm (deterministic validation followed by at most one deterministic repair when an unambiguous repair mapping existed). The preregistered primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) and the primary hypothesis test is the exact two‑sided McNemar (implemented as a two‑sided binomial on discordant pairs). Planned maximum hosted calls = 400; realized model_calls_used = 201 (200 shared initial generations + 1 deterministic repair invocation implemented in code, i.e., no extra LLM call). The preregistration also declared a target absolute effect of 0.15 for power calculations; those operating assumptions are discussed in the results and interpretation sections.

Task bank and scoring: The confirmatory bank contains 200 intent–expected‑configuration pairs created by a deterministic task generator. Each task payload specifies initial_state, expected_final_state, a required_sequence (authoritative ordered list of required commands), workflow policies (e.g., make‑before‑break, protected interfaces), and difficulty metadata. The scoring rule (full_intent_constraint_validation) requires that generated configurations: (a) parse into canonical CLI statements, (b) include the task’s required_sequence with correct presence and order, (c) respect dependency and group‑activity policies, (d) preserve protected‑interface values, and (e) when applied in the deterministic emulator produce an expected_final_state equal to the reference. Provider/API generation failures are treated per the preregistered missingness plan as arm failures; none occurred in the confirmatory run.

Deterministic validator: The guarded arm used a deterministic three‑stage validator that emits machine‑readable traces for scoring and repair logic. Stage 1 performs syntactic parsing and canonical normalization of CLI lines; unrecoverable syntax failures produce SYNTAX_PARSE_ERROR and block deterministic repair. Stage 2 checks structural and workflow constraints, deterministically verifying presence and ordering of required_sequence entries and enforcing dependency/group policies; emitted violation codes include MISSING_REQUIRED_COMMAND, DEPENDENCY_VIOLATION, PROTECTED_INTERFACE_MODIFICATION, and TRANSIENT_ORDER_VIOLATION. Stage 3 applies the normalized configuration in a Dockerized Mininet+FRR emulator and compares the observed final_state to the expected_final_state; validation_after.valid is reported only on exact final_state equality. Validator traces record parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, normalized_configuration, violation_codes/violation_count, and before/after validation summaries to support auditable failure‑mode analysis.

Deterministic repair operator and operational constraints: The preregistered repair operator is a rule‑based transformer invoked only when violation_count > 0 and the violation family belongs to a preregistered repairable set. Repairs obey three operational constraints: (i) no additional LLM calls (repairs are deterministic code transformations), (ii) bounded budget (≤1 repair attempt per episode in the confirmatory run), and (iii) an unambiguous mapping requirement (repairs applied only when a unique deterministic transformation can be computed from the task payload). Canonical transformations include insertion of missing required commands at canonical positions derived from required_sequence, deterministic stable reordering of annotated blocks to satisfy dependency rules, and deterministic enforcement to preserve protected fields. If multiple equally plausible deterministic repairs exist, the operator abstains and the episode remains unrepaired. All repair decisions and resulting normalized configurations were recorded for audit.
sections.results:
Execution and primary outcomes: The confirmatory run completed all planned episodes (completed_episode_count = 400) with no provider/API failures. Condition‑level results: baseline_successes = 199/200 (0.995), guarded_successes = 200/200 (1.000). The paired contingency is n11 = 199, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005.

Exact‑test and interval estimates: The preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test reduces to a two‑sided binomial on discordant pairs with n = n10 + n01 = 1 and k = n10 = 1; the resulting two‑sided p‑value is p = 1.0. Because asymptotic chi‑square approximations are invalid for such small discordant counts, the exact formulation was used as preregistered. Complementary uncertainty quantification used a paired‑bootstrap percentile CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729), yielding a 95% CI = [0.0, 0.015]. Under the preregistered power plan (target absolute effect = 0.15) the observed CI excludes the planned target because the baseline was near‑ceiling; this ceiling reduced discordant pair counts and therefore inferential sensitivity.

Repair and diagnostic accounting: The validator reported validation_before.valid == false in exactly one confirmatory episode. Deterministic repair invocations = 1 and that single deterministic repair converted the episode into a validator‑passing final configuration, producing the sole guarded‑only success (n10 = 1). Provider‑call accounting records hosted_model_call_event_count = 201 with stage counts shared_initial_generation = 200 and repair = 1. Aggregated per‑task difficulty labels across the confirmatory bank are: easy = 20, medium = 80, hard = 60, very_hard = 40 (sum = 200). The single repaired episode that produced the solitary guarded‑only success corresponds to task_id task-000137 in the archived manifest; the validator emitted violation_codes = ["MISSING_REQUIRED_COMMAND"], the deterministic repair applied an insertion of the missing required command at the canonical position derived from required_sequence, and validation_before.valid → validation_after.valid transitioned from false to true. All run traces, including the repair decision and before/after normalized configurations, are preserved in the archived evidence bundle for audit.
sections.discussion:
Operational interpretation: Under the shared_initial_candidate estimand and the curated confirmatory distribution the ungated gpt‑5‑mini generator produced near‑perfect candidates (199/200). Deterministic validators provide structured violation codes that enable narrowly targeted deterministic repairs; in this low‑error regime the marginal yield of a conservative single‑step rule‑based repair on the same candidate is small but auditable and low cost (one repair invocation, no additional LLM calls). For practitioners constrained by model‑call budgets and stringent auditability requirements, the shared‑candidate guarded design preserves low hosted‑call cost while offering an assurance gate with machine‑readable failure explanations.

Statistical sensitivity and design trade‑offs: The preregistered primary test (exact McNemar) is appropriate for paired binary outcomes; however, its power depends on discordant pair counts. The near‑ceiling baseline limited discordant events (n = 1), producing an uninterpretable two‑sided p = 1.0 for rejecting the null of equal marginal proportions while the paired‑bootstrap CI [0.0, 0.015] quantifies plausible paired differences. Practical recommendations follow: (i) when baseline performance is near ceiling, detectability of moderate absolute improvements requires larger sample sizes or altered task distributions with more failure modes; (ii) if operational budgets permit, independent resampling (multiple independent LLM draws per intent) or LLM‑invoked iterative repair loops will likely increase yield at the expense of higher provider costs and more complex governance/audit considerations; (iii) deterministic validators remain valuable regardless of marginal repair yield because they enable auditable rejection, targeted repair or escalation, and deterministic rollback triggers.

Failure‑mode diagnostics and implications: The recorded failure taxonomy in the single unrepaired episode was a missing required command that a deterministic canonical insertion remedied unambiguously. Across the confirmatory bank syntactic/parse failures = 0, suggesting that most remaining small failure modes in this synthetic curated set were structural (missing lines, order violations) rather than low‑level parsing errors. However, emulator fidelity limitations remain: deterministic emulation cannot fully capture runtime phenomena such as BGP convergence timing, transient control‑plane races, or vendor firmware corner cases. Consequently, some failures that appear corrected in the emulator might still exhibit risk in a production device fleet; conversely, some emulator‑reported failures attributable to convergence timing may be operationally benign if observed in situ with realistic timers. These factors constrain external validity.

Design guidance: For low‑cost, auditable NetOps automation where model‑call budgets or governance constraints dominate, shared‑candidate guarded designs (single initial generation + deterministic validator ± deterministic repair) are attractive. Where maximizing pass rates is paramount—and additional model calls are affordable—practitioners should consider independent‑resampling, multi‑hypothesis ensembles, or LLM‑guided iterative repair. In all cases we recommend deterministic, machine‑readable validators as mandatory assurance machinery for repeatability, auditability, and low‑latency failure explanations.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, autonomy‑locked paired experiment to measure whether a bounded deterministic generate–verify–repair guard improves emulator‑executable success for LLM‑generated NetOps configurations under a shared‑candidate budget. Ungated gpt‑5‑mini generation succeeded in 199/200 confirmatory cases; the deterministic guarded pipeline succeeded in 200/200. The observed paired difference = 0.005 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.015]) does not support the preregistered 0.15 absolute‑effect target because the baseline was near ceiling. Deterministic repair‑on‑the‑same‑candidate yielded negligible marginal improvement in this estimand and task distribution, yet deterministic validators remain valuable, auditable assurance gates in operational NetOps pipelines. The archived evidence bundle contains full run traces, validator and repair traces (including the single repair trace), and analysis artifacts for independent audit and reanalysis.

disclosure_statement:
This study was executed autonomously after an autonomy lock defined by the initial master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA-256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human involvement prior to the lock was limited to selecting the topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and approving the master prompt. No manual human editing of technical content, figures, captions, references, results, or manuscript text occurred after the lock. The autonomous pipeline performed literature search and verification, research‑gap selection, preregistration (study_id cnd-001-5f3a), code generation, experiment execution, artifact capture, analysis, internal critique, peer‑review checks, and manuscript drafting.

Models and tooling: Generation requested gpt-5-mini. Validation used a deterministic netops validator implementing syntactic parsing, structural/workflow checks, and deterministic emulator application. Repairs in the confirmatory run were applied by deterministic code only (no additional LLM calls). The execution environment used a Dockerized Mininet+FRR emulator orchestrated by the study adapter. Preregistered and enforced settings (not altered post-lock) include: primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; confirmatory sample = n=200 paired intents; maximum model-call budget = 400; repair budget ≤ 1 deterministic repair iteration; primary analysis = exact McNemar two‑sided (exact‑binomial on discordant pairs); bootstrap CIs = 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729. Execution accounting: the run completed 400 episodes with model_calls_used = 201 (shared_initial_generation = 200; deterministic repair_stage invocations = 1). All prompts, provider‑call traces, responses, validator traces, repair traces (the single invoked repair trace), analysis artifacts, and the execution manifest are archived in the study evidence bundle.
limitations: Synthetic, curated confirmatory task bank focused on small single‑ and multi‑device changes; not comprehensive of production NetOps workloads (multivendor CLI dialects, hardware idiosyncrasies, dynamic control‑plane timing).
Single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) evaluated; findings do not imply multi‑model generality.
Deterministic emulator + validator model control‑plane behavior but cannot fully capture real‑world runtime dynamics such as BGP convergence timing or vendor‑specific runtime effects.
Preregistered repair budget limited to a single deterministic repair iteration; different repair strategies or additional iterations might yield different outcomes.
Shared‑initial‑generation design reduces model‑call cost and isolates repair‑on‑same‑candidate effectiveness but reduces external generalizability compared with independent‑resampling estimands.
Near‑ceiling baseline success limited statistical power to analyze failure‑mode distributions in the confirmatory set; exploratory failure‑taxonomy conclusions are therefore constrained.
Adversarial or out‑of‑distribution intents (e.g., jailbreaks, malformed ambiguous intents) were not included in the confirmatory set and require separate evaluation.
Full per‑task difficulty labels and all run traces are archived in the study evidence bundle for audit and per‑task inspection.
